title: Blistering Diseases
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: A blister forms wherever the proteins that hold skin together fail, and the depth of that failure decides everything a board question can show you. This chapter works through the adhesion apparatus of the epidermis and the dermal-epidermal junction, then uses it to explain the inherited blistering diseases (epidermolysis bullosa) and the autoantibody-mediated ones (pemphigus vulgaris, pemphigus foliaceus, bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis). Questions give you an age, a blister that is tense or flaccid, the presence or absence of oral erosions, a histologic split level, and an immunofluorescence pattern. Each of those findings follows from one target protein and its position in the skin.
prerequisites: Layers of the epidermis and the normal keratinocyte differentiation sequence (IN-1)
Structure of desmosomes, hemidesmosomes, and the basement membrane zone, including cadherins and integrins
Collagen types and their tissue distribution, especially types IV and VII
Antibody classes and effector functions, including complement activation and Fc receptor recruitment of granulocytes
Type II hypersensitivity and the genetics of HLA-linked autoimmunity

connections.how: The adhesion proteins taught as normal histology are the exact antigens and gene products that fail in every disease in this chapter.
Pemphigus is a type II reaction in which antibody binding alone disrupts function, while pemphigoid and dermatitis herpetiformis add complement and granulocyte recruitment.
Dermatitis herpetiformis is the cutaneous expression of gluten-sensitive enteropathy, sharing HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 and the transglutaminase antigen family.

sections.title: Adhesion architecture of the skin and the types of epidermolysis bullosa

blocks.text: Skin resists shear through two sets of junctions arranged in series. Keratinocytes bind to one another at desmosomes, whose transmembrane cadherins are desmoglein 1 and desmoglein 3 linked inside the cell to plakoglobin, plakophilin, desmoplakin, and the keratin intermediate filament network. Basal keratinocytes bind downward to the basement membrane at hemidesmosomes, built on integrin alpha-6 beta-4 with the transmembrane protein BP180 (also called collagen XVII) and the intracellular plakin BP230. Beneath the basal cell lies the lamina lucida, crossed by laminin 332, then the lamina densa of type IV collagen, and finally the anchoring fibrils of type VII collagen looping into the papillary dermis.

Because these elements sit at fixed depths, the identity of the broken protein fixes the level of the split, and the level of the split fixes the clinical appearance. A split high in the epidermis leaves a thin roof that tears almost immediately, so the lesion is a flaccid blister or a bare erosion. A split beneath the whole epidermis leaves a full-thickness roof and a tense dome. A split at or below the lamina densa injures dermal matrix, so healing proceeds through fibrosis and leaves scars, milia, and contractures.

blocks.text: Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of inherited diseases in which one of these proteins is absent or defective from birth. In simplex disease the keratin 5 and keratin 14 filament scaffold of basal keratinocytes collapses under friction and those cells cytolyse, so the split is intraepidermal and healing is usually scar free. In junctional disease, loss of laminin 332 or of collagen XVII removes the link that crosses the lamina lucida, so the skin separates in that layer. In dystrophic disease, reduced or absent type VII collagen leaves no anchoring fibrils, so the split falls below the lamina densa within the uppermost dermis and every blister is a dermal wound.

blocks.title: Major types of epidermolysis bullosa
rows: Intermediate filament scaffold of basal cells
Laminin 332 or collagen XVII (LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2, COL17A1)
Hemidesmosome anchor across the lamina lucida
Anchoring fibrils into the papillary dermis
blocks.caption: The split descends as the defective protein sits deeper, which is why scarring is a feature of dystrophic disease and not of simplex disease.

blocks.text: Two points guard against common errors. First, a split within basal cells is still intraepidermal, so simplex disease is not a subepidermal blistering disease despite being so fragile. Second, type VII collagen is the shared antigen of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa and of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita; the first is a mutation in the gene, the second an IgG autoantibody against the protein in an adult, which is why the acquired form has no family history and shows immunoglobulin on biopsy.

blocks.predict: A newborn has widespread blisters, and electron microscopy places the plane of separation in the lamina lucida. Which proteins are candidates, and would you expect scarring?
blocks.explain: Laminin 332 and collagen XVII cross the lamina lucida, so either can be defective. The split lies above the lamina densa, so dermal matrix is largely spared and scarring is less prominent than in dystrophic disease, although erosions in severe generalized junctional disease still carry high infant mortality.

sections.title: Clinical course of epidermolysis bullosa and the consequences of dermal splitting

blocks.text: The defect is present in every keratinocyte from conception, so disease appears with the first mechanical stress: blisters and erosions at birth or in early infancy, at sites of handling, rubbing of clothing, crawling, or the pressure of nursing. The distribution follows friction rather than any immunologic pattern, favoring hands, feet, knees, elbows, and the occiput, and new lesions can be produced deliberately by rubbing. Because the same proteins are expressed in all stratified squamous epithelium and in nail and tooth structures, mucosal erosions, nail dystrophy or loss, and enamel defects accompany the skin disease in the more severe forms.

Severity tracks the split level and the amount of residual protein. In simplex disease, blisters are localized or generalized but intraepidermal, so re-epithelialization from intact basal cells and adnexa is efficient and scarring is unusual; localized disease in particular tends to become less troublesome after childhood. In severe generalized junctional disease, loss of laminin 332 leaves extensive nonhealing erosions, exuberant granulation tissue around the nares and mouth, laryngeal and tracheal involvement, protein and fluid loss, failure to thrive, and sepsis, which together account for death in infancy in the most severe cases.

Recessive dystrophic disease is where the consequences of splitting below the lamina densa become visible over years. Each blister is a dermal wound, and repeated wounding in the absence of anchoring fibrils heals by fibrosis. Scar contracture fuses the fingers into a mitten deformity (pseudosyndactyly) and flexes the joints, nails are lost, and milia appear where sweat ducts and follicles are occluded by scar. Mucosal involvement scars as well, producing esophageal strictures with dysphagia and secondary malnutrition, microstomia, and ankyloglossia, while corneal erosions scar the eye. Anemia, growth failure, and dilated cardiomyopathy follow from chronic inflammation and nutritional deficiency.

blocks.title: Why recessive dystrophic disease ends in carcinoma
steps: Absent type VII collagen, sublamina densa split

blocks.caption: Carcinoma arises in chronic wounds rather than at random, which is why risk rises steeply from the second and third decades.

blocks.text: The squamous cell carcinoma of recessive dystrophic disease behaves unlike the sun-induced squamous cell carcinoma of elderly skin. It arises in chronically wounded, scarred, usually sun-protected sites on the hands, arms, and legs, often before age 30, and metastasizes early despite being well differentiated histologically, so it is the leading cause of death in these patients by middle adulthood. Dominant dystrophic disease is milder, with blistering and nail dystrophy over bony prominences, albopapuloid lesions (pale firm papules over the trunk), and much less risk.

sections.title: Bullous pemphigoid: hemidesmosomal antigens, complement, and the tense subepidermal blister

blocks.text: Bullous pemphigoid is the most common autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease and a disease of later life, with most patients older than about 60 years and incidence rising steeply with age. The autoantibodies are IgG against two hemidesmosomal proteins: BP180 (collagen XVII), a transmembrane protein whose extracellular NC16A domain is the dominant pathogenic epitope, and BP230, an intracellular plakin that links the hemidesmosome plaque to keratin filaments. Antibody against the NC16A domain of BP180 correlates with disease activity, which fits the fact that only this epitope is accessible to circulating antibody from outside the cell.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of bullous pemphigoid
steps: IgG binds the NC16A domain of BP180 at the hemidesmosome
Classical complement activation deposits C3 along the basement membrane
C5a and mast cell degranulation recruit eosinophils and neutrophils
Granulocyte elastase, gelatinase B, and tryptase degrade BP180 and matrix
Basal cells detach from the basement membrane, producing a subepidermal split
Exposed antigen and continued inflammation sustain further antibody binding
blocks.caption: An antibody plus complement plus granulocyte protease mechanism, which is why eosinophils are conspicuous in the blister and the dermal infiltrate.

blocks.text: The clinical picture follows directly from the depth of this split. Separation occurs beneath the entire epidermis, so the roof of the blister is full thickness and mechanically strong: bullae are tense, dome shaped, up to several centimeters, and persist for days before eroding, and lateral pressure on normal-looking adjacent skin does not shear the epidermis, so the Nikolsky sign is negative. Lesions favor the flexures, lower abdomen, inner thighs, groin, and forearms, and are intensely pruritic. Many patients pass through a prodromal phase of weeks to months with urticarial plaques, eczematous patches, or pruritus alone before any blister forms, which is explained by inflammation at the junction preceding frank separation. Oral involvement occurs in a minority, roughly 10 to 20 percent of patients, and when it does the erosions are limited and rarely the presenting complaint. Healing is without scarring, because the split lies above the dermal matrix, although postinflammatory pigment change is common.

Diagnosis rests on three levels of evidence that each reflect the mechanism. Light microscopy of a fresh blister shows a subepidermal blister with an intact epidermal roof and no acantholysis, with eosinophils in the blister cavity and a perivascular dermal infiltrate rich in eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows a smooth linear band of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone, the morphologic signature of antibody bound to a single continuous structure. On salt-split normal skin the patient's serum labels the epidermal roof, because BP180 and BP230 lie above the artificial plane of cleavage in the lamina lucida; this separates bullous pemphigoid from epidermolysis bullosa acquisita and from anti-laminin 332 disease, whose antigens lie below that plane and label the dermal floor.

Two variants reuse the same antigen and are worth recognizing. Pemphigoid gestationis presents with periumbilical urticarial lesions and blisters in the second or third trimester, driven by anti-BP180 generated against placental collagen XVII. Mucous membrane pemphigoid targets BP180 or laminin 332 and produces scarring erosions of oral, ocular, and genital mucosa, with conjunctival fibrosis and symblepharon; mucosal healing proceeds by fibrosis of the lamina propria, so scarring is the rule at these sites even though the split level is the same.

sections.title: Pemphigus vulgaris: desmoglein autoantibodies, acantholysis, and the tombstone basal layer

blocks.text: Pemphigus vulgaris is a type II hypersensitivity disease in which IgG, predominantly the IgG4 subclass, binds the extracellular domain of desmoglein 3, frequently with additional antibody against desmoglein 1. The antibody is pathogenic by itself: it does not need complement or granulocytes, and neonatal disease from transplacental IgG, which resolves as maternal antibody clears, demonstrates the point. Bound antibody interferes with desmoglein trans-interaction directly and also triggers signaling, including p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase activation, that causes keratin filament retraction and internalization of desmoglein from the cell surface. Adhesion between keratinocytes therefore fails, the cells round up and float apart, and this separation of cell from cell within the epidermis is acantholysis. The disease associates with the HLA class II alleles DRB1*04:02 and DQB1*05:03, and onset is typically in the fourth to sixth decades.

blocks.title: Pemphigus vulgaris from antibody to erosion
steps: IgG4 against desmoglein 3, often also desmoglein 1
Steric blockade plus p38 MAPK signaling and desmoglein internalization
Desmosomes disassemble; keratinocytes separate (acantholysis)
Suprabasal split; hemidesmosomes keep basal cells on the membrane
Thin-roofed flaccid bulla ruptures into a painful erosion
blocks.caption: No complement step is required, which distinguishes this mechanism from that of bullous pemphigoid.

blocks.text: The split sits immediately above the basal layer because desmoglein 3 is expressed most heavily in the lower epidermis, while the basal cells remain anchored downward by hemidesmosomes, which the antibody does not touch. Histology therefore shows a suprabasal blister whose floor is a single row of basal keratinocytes still attached to the basement membrane but separated from one another, each left standing on its narrow base: the row of tombstones. Rounded acantholytic keratinocytes float in the cavity, and a cytologic smear from the base of a fresh lesion (Tzanck preparation) shows these cells.

Clinically, mucosal surfaces declare the disease first in the great majority of patients. Oral erosions, painful enough to limit eating, precede skin lesions by weeks to months, and because mucosa depends on desmoglein 3 and blister roofs there are rubbed off at once, intact blisters are almost never seen in the mouth. Skin lesions are flaccid, easily ruptured bullae on the scalp, face, trunk, axillae, and groin that leave weeping, crusted, slow-healing erosions. The Nikolsky sign is positive: lateral pressure on uninvolved skin shears the epidermis, since the acantholytic plane is present in skin that still looks normal. Pressure on an intact bulla spreads it into adjacent skin (the Asboe-Hansen sign). Extensive erosion causes fluid and protein loss and allows bacterial invasion, which made untreated disease highly lethal before immunosuppression was available.

Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows IgG, often with C3, outlining the surface of every keratinocyte through the epidermis, producing the net-like or fishnet pattern; the antibody is deposited on cell membranes rather than along one line, which is exactly what the net pattern means. Indirect immunofluorescence on monkey esophagus substrate detects circulating antibody, and titers track activity. Paraneoplastic pemphigus is the exception to remember: antibodies against plakins (envoplakin and periplakin) as well as desmogleins, severe intractable stomatitis, lichenoid skin lesions, and sometimes bronchiolitis obliterans, occurring with Castleman disease or non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

blocks.predict: If antibody bound only desmoglein 1 and spared desmoglein 3, where would the split fall and would the mouth be involved?
blocks.explain: Desmoglein 1 is concentrated in the superficial epidermis and is not the dominant desmoglein in mucosa, so the split would be subcorneal and the mouth spared. That is pemphigus foliaceus, covered in the next section.

sections.title: Distinguishing pemphigus vulgaris, pemphigus foliaceus, and bullous pemphigoid

blocks.text: All three diseases are IgG mediated, and all three can present with erosions in an adult, so they are separated by one question asked four ways: which protein is the target, and therefore at what depth does the skin split, how tense is the blister, is mucosa involved, and what shape does the deposited antibody make. Desmoglein compensation explains the mucosal column. Mucosa expresses desmoglein 3 with little desmoglein 1, so losing desmoglein 3 blisters the mouth; the superficial epidermis expresses mainly desmoglein 1, so losing desmoglein 1 blisters superficial skin but leaves mucosa adequately held by its abundant desmoglein 3.

blocks.title: Comparison of the three IgG-mediated blistering diseases
rows: Subcorneal, at or just below the granular layer
Fourth to sixth decades; scalp, face, trunk, flexures
Middle age; seborrheic areas of face, scalp, upper trunk
Usually over 60 years; flexures, abdomen, thighs
Eosinophils in blister and dermis, no acantholysis
Net-like intercellular IgG through the epidermis
Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane
blocks.caption: Target antigen determines every other row; the immunofluorescence shape simply reports whether antibody lies around cells or along one line.

blocks.text: Pemphigus foliaceus deserves its own description, since its appearance misleads. The split is so superficial that intact blisters are seldom seen; patients present with scaly, crusted, sometimes exfoliative erosions in a seborrheic distribution on the face, scalp, and upper trunk, and the disease can be mistaken for seborrheic dermatitis or widespread impetigo. There is no oral disease. An endemic form, fogo selvagem, occurs in clusters in rural Brazil, with anti-desmoglein 1 antibody arising after insect bite exposure, which illustrates environmental triggering of autoimmunity.

blocks.title: Worked example: two subcorneal splits with different causes
blocks.text: A three-year-old has fever and diffuse tender erythema, then superficial sheets of skin peel with gentle pressure. A forty-five-year-old has months of scaly crusted erosions on the face and upper back with the same subcorneal split on biopsy. Both lose desmoglein 1, so both split at the same level and both shear under pressure. In the child, staphylococcal exfoliative toxin A or B is a protease that cleaves desmoglein 1 directly, so onset is acute, there is systemic toxicity, and direct immunofluorescence is negative. In the adult, IgG binds desmoglein 1, so the course is chronic and immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG. Same protein, same plane, different agent: enzyme versus antibody.

Two further distinctions avoid errors. A positive Nikolsky sign is not specific to pemphigus; it is also positive in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and in Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, where keratinocyte necrosis rather than acantholysis destroys cohesion, and immunofluorescence there is negative. Among the subepidermal diseases, immunofluorescence shape separates the group: linear IgG and C3 indicates bullous pemphigoid or epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (separated by salt-split skin, epidermal roof versus dermal floor), linear IgA alone indicates linear IgA bullous dermatosis, and granular IgA in the papillae indicates dermatitis herpetiformis.

sections.title: Dermatitis herpetiformis: IgA against epidermal transglutaminase and the celiac connection

blocks.text: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin expression of gluten-sensitive enteropathy. In people carrying HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8, deamidated gliadin peptides presented by those class II molecules drive a T cell dependent IgA response against tissue transglutaminase (TG2) in the intestine. The response broadens to the closely homologous epidermal transglutaminase (TG3), a keratinocyte enzyme that cross-links proteins during cornification, and high-avidity IgA against TG3 is the serologic marker of the skin disease. Nearly all patients have celiac-type changes on small-bowel biopsy, ranging from an increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes to villous atrophy, yet most have no bowel symptoms, which is why the rash can be the only evidence of celiac disease.

blocks.title: Gut to skin in dermatitis herpetiformis
steps: Gluten peptides deamidated by tissue transglutaminase in the gut
HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 presentation drives IgA against TG2, then TG3
Circulating IgA and TG3 complexes deposit in dermal papillary tips
Neutrophils recruited, forming papillary microabscesses
Protease release splits the epidermis at the papillary tips
Grouped subepidermal vesicles with intense pruritus
blocks.caption: A single dietary antigen in the gut produces lesions in the skin through a shared enzyme family.

blocks.text: The eruption is intensely pruritic and burning, often enough that excoriations and crusts are all that remain by the time the patient is seen. Lesions are small, grouped (herpetiform) vesicles and urticarial papules distributed symmetrically over extensor surfaces: elbows, knees, buttocks, shoulders, sacrum, and the posterior scalp. Mucosal lesions are rare. The disease is chronic and relapsing, more common in adults of northern European ancestry, and iodine exposure can provoke a flare. Associated autoimmune disease, especially autoimmune thyroid disease, and the small-bowel lymphoma risk of celiac disease both travel with it.

Histology and immunofluorescence follow the deposition pattern. Early lesional skin shows collections of neutrophils with fibrin at the tips of the dermal papillae, the papillary microabscesses, with vacuolar change and then small subepidermal vesicles as the papillary tips separate; eosinophils may be present but are not the dominant cell, which distinguishes this from bullous pemphigoid. Direct immunofluorescence of normal-appearing perilesional skin, the preferred biopsy site, shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae, sometimes with C3. The deposits are granular rather than linear because IgA sits in clumps within the papillary tips instead of along a continuous basement membrane, and they persist for months after gluten is withdrawn, then fade, confirming that dietary antigen sustains the process.

rows: Linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane
Linear IgA at the basement membrane
LAD-1, a shed fragment of BP180

blocks.caption: Antibody class and the shape of the deposit separate four diseases that all split beneath the epidermis.

blocks.predict: A patient has itchy grouped vesicles on the elbows and knees, and direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgA along the basement membrane rather than granular IgA in the papillae. Is this dermatitis herpetiformis?
blocks.explain: No. Linear IgA indicates linear IgA bullous dermatosis, whose antigen is the LAD-1 fragment of BP180 and which has no gluten relationship; several cases are drug associated. The distribution can mimic dermatitis herpetiformis, so the immunofluorescence pattern, not the rash, decides.

integration.text: This chapter is histology turned into pathology. Each junction described in normal skin, the desmosome with its desmogleins, the hemidesmosome with BP180 and BP230, the laminin 332 of the lamina lucida, and the type VII collagen anchoring fibrils, is the target of a specific disease, and the depth of the target predicts blister tension, the Nikolsky sign, scarring, and the mucosal pattern. Genetics and immunology reach the same proteins by different routes: a mutation removes the protein from birth and gives a lifelong mechanical fragility, while an autoantibody blocks it in adulthood and gives an inflammatory disease with deposited immunoglobulin on biopsy. Type VII collagen illustrates both routes in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa and epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, and desmoglein 1 illustrates a third, enzymatic route when staphylococcal exfoliative toxin cleaves it in scalded skin syndrome.

The immunologic mechanisms are themselves worth contrasting, because they explain the histology. Pemphigus is antibody acting alone, a type II reaction in which binding and signaling disassemble a junction, so the infiltrate is sparse and acantholytic cells dominate. Bullous pemphigoid adds complement and granulocyte proteases, so eosinophils fill the blister. Dermatitis herpetiformis works through immune complexes of IgA and transglutaminase that recruit neutrophils, which is why its lesion begins as a papillary microabscess and why the deposits depend on continued exposure to a dietary antigen rather than on anything local to the skin. The biomedical limits are worth stating: immunofluorescence localizes antibody but does not prove it is pathogenic, antibody titers correlate imperfectly with activity, and reported frequencies such as mucosal involvement in bullous pemphigoid vary between series.

summary: The depth of the defective adhesion protein sets the split level, and the split level sets blister tension, scarring, and the Nikolsky sign.

Epidermolysis bullosa simplex breaks keratins 5 and 14 within basal cells, junctional disease breaks laminin 332 or collagen XVII in the lamina lucida, and dystrophic disease breaks type VII collagen below the lamina densa.

Epidermolysis bullosa blisters from minor friction at birth, with nail, enamel, and mucosal involvement in severe forms; recessive dystrophic disease scars into mitten hands and esophageal strictures and leads to aggressive squamous cell carcinoma in young adults.

Bullous pemphigoid is IgG against BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230 with complement activation and eosinophil recruitment, giving tense subepidermal bullae in older adults, a negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane.

Pemphigus vulgaris is IgG against desmoglein 3, often also desmoglein 1, acting without complement to cause suprabasal acantholysis with a tombstone basal row, flaccid bullae, early painful oral erosions, a positive Nikolsky sign, and net-like intercellular IgG.
Desmoglein compensation explains site: mucosa depends on desmoglein 3, superficial epidermis on desmoglein 1, so pemphigus foliaceus splits subcorneally and spares the mouth.
Salt-split skin separates linear IgG diseases: bullous pemphigoid labels the epidermal roof, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita the dermal floor.

Dermatitis herpetiformis is IgA against epidermal transglutaminase in gluten-sensitive enteropathy, with grouped pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces, neutrophilic microabscesses at papillary tips, and granular IgA in the dermal papillae.
A positive Nikolsky sign also occurs in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and in Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, where immunofluorescence is negative.
Acantholysis means separation of keratinocyte from keratinocyte and is intraepidermal; subepidermal diseases show no acantholysis.

Frequency of oral involvement in bullous pemphigoid is quoted from about 10 to 30 percent across series; this chapter uses about 10 to 20 percent.

The proportion of pemphigus vulgaris patients whose disease begins in the mouth is given as roughly 50 to 70 percent in some texts and as the majority in others; this chapter says the great majority without a figure.

Current epidermolysis bullosa classification recognizes four types (simplex, junctional, dystrophic, and Kindler epidermolysis bullosa, the last from FERMT1 mutation with mixed split levels). Confirm whether NABNE expects Kindler and the newer subtype names, or only the classic three.

Reported lifetime squamous cell carcinoma risk in severe recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (commonly cited as most patients by the fourth decade) varies by registry; no figure is stated here.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Nikolsky sign, Asboe-Hansen sign, Tzanck preparation, Herlitz and Hallopeau-Siemens subtypes, and fogo selvagem, or only descriptive terms.
HLA associations for pemphigus vulgaris (DRB1*04:02, DQB1*05:03) are population dependent; verify whether specific alleles are tested.

Whether bullous pemphigoid blistering requires complement is debated, since complement-independent pathways have been shown experimentally; this chapter teaches the complement-dependent model as the consensus with eosinophil proteases as effectors.

Texts differ on how many dermatitis herpetiformis patients show frank villous atrophy as opposed to milder enteropathy (figures from roughly two thirds to nearly all); this chapter states the range of findings rather than a percentage.
